lesson.title: will ≠ will
lesson.subtitle: English turned 'will' into a future machine — German kept its ancient job: wanting

hook.title: The Word English Broke
hook.content: In ancient Germanic, 'will' meant one thing: desire. English eventually bent it into a future-tense machine — 'it will rain' desires nothing. German never bent it. Ich will ein Bier is a confession of thirst, not a weather forecast. The proof lives inside English itself: free will, will to live, against my will, last will and testament. Every time you use those phrases, you are using German's will. And the twin of soll is shall — thou shalt not kill is, word for word, du sollst nicht töten.

footnotes.title: The World as Will
footnotes.content: Schopenhauer titled his masterwork Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1818) — 'The World as Will and Representation'. German philosophers could pick 'Wille' precisely because the word still meant raw wanting, the meaning English buried under its future tense.

footnotes.title: Thou Shalt ↔ Du Sollst
footnotes.content: Luther's Ten Commandments say Du sollst nicht töten; the King James Bible says Thou shalt not kill. Same verb, same ending, same commandment — preserved in two languages that otherwise let 'shall' and 'soll' drift apart.

pattern.title: The Desire Modals: wollen, sollen, mögen
pattern.content: ich will = I want (du willst, er will). ich soll = I am supposed to / shall (du sollst). ich mag = I like — the twin of English may/might, which also once meant 'to have the power to'. And ich möchte is its polite sibling: 'I would like'. Watch the endings: du willst keeps the Shakespearean -st (thou willest), and none of these ever takes zu before the infinitive — the desire travels bare: Ich will schwimmen. Meanwhile möchten softens desire into politeness: Ich möchte einen Kaffee — I would like a coffee.
pattern.linguist_note: All five modals drop the -t in the 3rd person exactly as English does: he can, he will, he must — never he cans. German: er kann, er will, er muss. A shared fossil of Proto-Germanic.

exercises.prompt: A friend says: 'Ich will ein Bier.' What did she tell you?
options: She wants a beer — right now
She will bring a beer someday
exercises.target_answer: She wants a beer — right now
exercises.meaning: ich will = I want (desire, not future)
exercises.explanation: German kept 'will' in its ancient desire sense — the meaning English preserves only in 'free will' and 'will to live'.

exercises.prompt: Match the desire modals with their English twins:
exercises.target_answer: ich will, du sollst, ich mag, wir müssen, ich habe Lust auf Kuchen, ich will die Wurst
exercises.meaning: I want, you shall, I like, we must, I feel like cake, I want the sausage
exercises.explanation: wollen ↔ will, sollen ↔ shall, mögen ↔ may — and die Lust is the desire noun hiding inside English 'lust'.

exercises.prompt: The beer costs twenty euro. Your verdict: 'zu teuer.' What does 'zu teuer' mean?
exercises.explanation: teuer is the true twin of English 'dear' — English d hardened to German t, then 'dear' drifted toward 'beloved' while teuer stayed with price. zu = too.

exercises.prompt: Express desire: 'Ich _____ schwimmen' (I want to swim):
exercises.meaning: Ich will schwimmen = I want to swim
exercises.explanation: ich will + bare infinitive — no zu, no future reading, just wanting.

exercises.idea: you and your friend are declaring a shared goal: you both want to learn German
cues: Who wants? → wir, so the modal takes -en: wir wollen
The bare infinitive closes the bracket: lernen goes last
exercises.explanation: wollen agrees with wir (-en) and the bare infinitive closes the bracket — desire travels bare, no zu.

summary.outcome: Use ich will / ich möchte for desire and never misread a German 'will' as the future.

use_example.german: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, und du willst ein Bier.
use_example.english: I would like a coffee, and you want a beer.

summary.takeaway: German will = want (free will), soll = shall, mag = may — the desire modals English bent or buried.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the modal bracket out in the wild — how 'Ich kann morgen kommen' packs three facts into one frame.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from will ≠ will (We want to learn German):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir wollen Deutsch lernen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of will ≠ will without relying on short-term echo.

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

sollen.etymology_derivation: Direct twin of English "shall" and "should" (Shakespeare: "thou shalt" ↔ German "du sollst").

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

mögen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "may" and "might" (Proto-Germanic *maganą). Subjunctive: möchte (would like).

lust.context_translation: I feel like having ice cream.
lust.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lustuz — the explicit twin of English lust; in German it just means desire (Lust haben). [wiktionary]

teuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *diurijaz — the true twin of English dear (d → t). [wiktionary]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

bier.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *beuzą. Medial ie produces pure tense monophthong [iː].

kuchen.context_translation: Would you like a piece of cake?
kuchen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōkô; Wiktionary names only Dutch koek — see Apfelkuchen. [wiktionary]

wurst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wursti; English wurst is only a later borrowing from German — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

weniger.etymology_derivation: Comparative of wenig, built on the Proto-Germanic root *wainagaz that Wiktionary ties to English woe: from woe-like, miserable to few and less. [wiktionary]

mikrowelle.context_phrase: Die Suppe ist in der Mikrowelle.
mikrowelle.context_translation: The soup is in the microwave.
mikrowelle.etymology_derivation: Compound of the Greek loan prefix mikro- and Welle, meaning wave; Mikro- is the same Greek element as English micro-. [wiktionary]

auch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *auk — the same word as the archaic English eke 'also', as in to eke out; English let it fade, German kept auch. [wiktionary]

münze.context_phrase: Ich habe nur eine Münze dabei.
münze.context_translation: I only have one coin with me.
münze.etymology_derivation: Through Proto-West Germanic *munit from Latin moneta, the coin-word that also became English money and mint. [wiktionary]

dusche.context_translation: I will take a quick shower.
dusche.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via French douche from Italian doccia — the same French word English took as douche; German replaced the older Brausebad over its bad connotations. [wiktionary]
